items.stem: Which apparatus is used to measure the volume of gas produced in a reaction?
items.answer: A gas syringe
items.markingKey: A gas syringe collects and measures gas volume (or an inverted measuring cylinder).

items.stem: Explain why the rate of reaction between marble chips and acid decreases as the reaction goes on.
items.answer: The reactants are being used up, so there are fewer acid particles and less marble to collide; collisions become less frequent.
items.markingKey: reactants used up [1]; fewer collisions [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why a cotton wool plug is placed in the neck of the flask when measuring mass loss.
items.answer: It lets the gas escape but stops acid spray escaping, so only the mass of gas lost is measured.
items.markingKey: gas escapes [1]; acid spray retained [1] [2]

items.stem: Zara adds limestone chips to dilute hydrochloric acid and collects the carbon dioxide in a gas syringe: 0 s: 0 cm³, 15 s: 43 cm³, 30 s: 67 cm³, 45 s: 80 cm³, 60 s: 87 cm³, 75 s: 91 cm³, 90 s: 93 cm³. Calculate the mean rate of reaction over the first 30 s.
items.answer: 2.23 cm³/s

items.stem: Diego adds magnesium ribbon to dilute hydrochloric acid and collects the hydrogen in a gas syringe: 0 s: 0 cm³, 20 s: 61 cm³, 40 s: 83 cm³, 60 s: 91 cm³, 80 s: 94 cm³, 100 s: 95 cm³, 120 s: 96 cm³. (a) Calculate the mean rate over the first 20 s and between 40 s and 60 s. (b) Explain why the rate changes.
items.answer: (a) 3.05 cm³/s and 0.4 cm³/s (b) The rate decreases because the reactants are being used up, so collisions become less frequent.
items.markingKey: (a) 61 ÷ 20 = 3.05 [1]; (91 − 83) ÷ 20 = 0.4 [1] (b) reactants used up / fewer collisions [1] [3]

items.stem: A class in Dubai reacts zinc granules with dilute sulfuric acid and measures the hydrogen given off: 0 s: 0 cm³, 20 s: 51 cm³, 40 s: 69 cm³, 60 s: 76 cm³, 80 s: 79 cm³, 100 s: 79 cm³, 120 s: 80 cm³. (a) Draw a labelled diagram, or describe, the apparatus used. (b) Describe a test to identify the gas.
items.answer: (a) Conical flask with the reactants and a bung connected by a delivery tube to a gas syringe; a stopwatch. (b) Hydrogen: a lighted splint gives a squeaky pop.
items.markingKey: (a) flask and bung [1]; gas syringe / measuring cylinder [1] [2] (b) test [1]; result [1] [2]

items.stem: Why does the mass of a flask of marble chips and acid decrease during the reaction?
items.answer: Carbon dioxide gas escapes
items.markingKey: The gas leaves through the cotton wool plug, so mass falls.

items.stem: Explain why a gas syringe gives more accurate results than counting bubbles.
items.answer: It measures the actual volume of gas; bubbles vary in size and fast bubbling is hard to count.
items.markingKey: measures volume [1]; bubbles vary / hard to count [1] [2]

items.stem: Mei claims: "The reaction is fastest at the end because the most gas has been collected by then." Do you agree? Explain your answer.
items.answer: No. The total volume is largest at the end, but the rate (gas per second) is greatest at the start, where the graph is steepest.
items.markingKey: total vs rate [1]; steepest at start [1] [2]

items.stem: Aisha places a flask of dilute hydrochloric acid and marble chips on a balance: 0 min: 175.20 g, 1 min: 174.68 g, 2 min: 174.30 g, 3 min: 174.01 g, 4 min: 173.80 g, 5 min: 173.65 g, 6 min: 173.53 g. Calculate the mass lost in the first 2 minutes and the mean rate of mass loss in g/min.

Omar adds limestone chips to dilute hydrochloric acid and collects the carbon dioxide in a gas syringe: 0 s: 0 cm³, 15 s: 63 cm³, 30 s: 82 cm³, 45 s: 88 cm³, 60 s: 89 cm³, 75 s: 90 cm³, 90 s: 90 cm³. (a) Calculate the mean rate over the first 15 s and between 30 s and 45 s. (b) Explain why the rate changes. (c) Describe how the graph of these results would look. (d) Suggest why the final volume might be slightly less than expected.
items.answer: (a) 4.2 cm³/s and 0.4 cm³/s (b) The rate decreases because the reactants are being used up, so collisions become less frequent. (c) A curve that is steep at the start, becomes less steep and levels off. (d) Some carbon dioxide escaped before the bung was fitted, or some dissolved in the solution.
items.markingKey: (a) 63 ÷ 15 = 4.2 [1]; (88 − 82) ÷ 15 = 0.4 [1] (b) reactants used up / fewer collisions [1] (c) [1] (d) gas lost / dissolved [1] [5]

items.stem: Nadia follows the reaction of zinc granules with dilute sulfuric acid using a gas syringe: 0 s: 0 cm³, 20 s: 46 cm³, 40 s: 62 cm³, 60 s: 68 cm³, 80 s: 71 cm³, 100 s: 72 cm³, 120 s: 72 cm³. (a) Explain, in terms of particles, why the rate decreases over time. (b) Suggest one source of error and how to reduce it.
items.answer: (a) Reacting particles are used up, so there are fewer particles to collide and fewer successful collisions per second. (b) Gas escapes while the bung is put in: use a divided flask or tie the solid in a bag so the reaction starts after sealing.
items.markingKey: (a) particles used up [1]; fewer collisions per second [1] [2] (b) error [1]; improvement [1] [2]

items.stem: Yusuf follows the reaction of zinc granules with dilute sulfuric acid using a gas syringe: 0 s: 0 cm³, 20 s: 42 cm³, 40 s: 55 cm³, 60 s: 58 cm³, 80 s: 60 cm³, 100 s: 60 cm³, 120 s: 60 cm³. (a) Calculate the mean rate of reaction in the first 20 s. (b) Describe a test to identify the gas. (c) Suggest one source of error and how to reduce it.
items.answer: (a) 2.1 cm³/s (b) Hydrogen: a lighted splint gives a squeaky pop. (c) Gas escapes while the bung is put in: use a divided flask or tie the solid in a bag so the reaction starts after sealing.
items.markingKey: (a) 42 ÷ 20 [1] = 2.1 cm³/s [1] [2] (b) test [1]; result [1] [2] (c) error [1]; improvement [1] [2]

items.stem: Which form of calcium carbonate reacts fastest with acid?
items.answer: Powder
items.markingKey: Powder has the largest surface area.

items.stem: Explain, using the particle model, why powdered marble reacts faster with acid than marble chips.
items.answer: Powder has a larger surface area, so more calcium carbonate particles are exposed to acid particles, giving more frequent collisions.
items.markingKey: larger surface area [1]; more frequent collisions [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why the total volume of gas is the same for chips and powder if the same mass is used with excess acid.
items.answer: The same amount of reactant is present, so the same amount of product forms; only the rate differs.
items.markingKey: same amount of reactant [1]; only rate changes [1] [2]

items.stem: A cube of calcium carbonate has sides of 6 cm. Calculate its total surface area.
items.answer: 216 cm²

items.stem: A cube of calcium carbonate has sides of 4 cm. It is cut into 8 identical smaller cubes, each with sides of 2 cm. (a) Calculate the surface area of the large cube. (b) Calculate the total surface area of all the small cubes. (c) Explain how this affects the rate of reaction with acid.
items.answer: (a) 96 cm² (b) 8 × 6 × 2² = 192 cm² (2 times larger) (c) Larger surface area exposes more particles, so collisions are more frequent and the reaction is faster.
items.markingKey: (a) 96 [1] (b) 192 cm² [1] (c) more collisions / faster [1] [3]

items.stem: In a flour mill in Lagos, a safety officer warns that fine flour dust in the air could explode. (a) Explain why fine dust burns much faster than a solid block of the same material. (b) Explain whether the total volume of gas produced depends on the form used.
items.answer: (a) Dust has a huge surface area in contact with oxygen, so combustion is extremely fast and can be explosive. (b) No: the same mass contains the same amount of reactant, so the total is the same; only the rate changes.
items.markingKey: (a) huge surface area [1]; very fast combustion [1] [2] (b) same total [1]; same amount of reactant [1] [2]

items.stem: Increasing the surface area of a solid reactant …
items.answer: increases the rate of reaction
items.markingKey: More particles exposed, more frequent collisions.

items.stem: Explain why small pieces of wood (kindling) are used to start a fire.
items.answer: Small pieces have a large surface area, so they react with oxygen faster and catch fire more easily.
items.markingKey: large surface area [1]; faster reaction with oxygen [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why indigestion tablets that are crushed work faster than whole ones.
items.answer: Crushing increases the surface area, so the tablet reacts with stomach acid faster.
items.markingKey: larger surface area [1]; faster neutralisation [1] [2]

items.stem: Jonas claims: "Powder reacts faster because it has more mass than the lumps." Do you agree? Explain your answer.
items.answer: No. The masses are the same; powder reacts faster because it has a larger surface area, so collisions are more frequent.
items.markingKey: same mass [1]; surface area / collisions [1] [2]

items.stem: Isla reacts 5 g of calcium carbonate with excess acid and times how long it takes to collect 60 cm³ of carbon dioxide: large lumps 200 s, small chips 90 s, powder 30 s. Calculate the mean rate of reaction for the lumps and for the powder.
items.answer: 0.3 cm³/s and 2 cm³/s

items.stem: Nadia compares how quickly whole and crushed antacid tablets react with dilute acid. (a) Suggest one advantage and one disadvantage of a fast-acting powder. (b) Explain whether the total volume of gas produced depends on the form used.
items.answer: (a) Advantage: relieves symptoms quickly. Disadvantage: harder to measure a dose, may fizz over, absorbs moisture from air. (b) No: the same mass contains the same amount of reactant, so the total is the same; only the rate changes.
items.markingKey: (a) advantage [1]; disadvantage [1] [2] (b) same total [1]; same amount of reactant [1] [2]

items.stem: In a flour mill in Manila, a safety officer warns that fine flour dust in the air could explode. (a) Describe an experiment to compare the rates for the different forms. (b) Explain whether the total volume of gas produced depends on the form used.
items.answer: (a) Add the same mass of each form to the same volume and concentration of acid at the same temperature; measure the gas volume (or mass loss) at regular intervals. (b) No: the same mass contains the same amount of reactant, so the total is the same; only the rate changes.
items.markingKey: (a) same mass / acid / temperature [1]; measure gas or mass over time [1]; compare rates [1] [3] (b) same total [1]; same amount of reactant [1] [2]

items.stem: What happens to the rate of most reactions when the temperature is increased?
items.answer: It increases
items.markingKey: Particles move faster and collide more often and with more energy.

items.stem: Explain, in terms of particles, why magnesium reacts faster with warm acid than with cold acid.
items.answer: At a higher temperature the acid particles move faster, so they collide with the magnesium more often and more collisions have enough energy to react.
items.markingKey: faster particles / more frequent collisions [1]; more energetic collisions [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why food cooks faster in a pressure cooker, where water boils at about 120 °C.
items.answer: The higher temperature makes the cooking reactions faster.
items.markingKey: higher temperature [1]; faster reactions [1] [2]

items.stem: Grace mixes sodium thiosulfate solution with dilute hydrochloric acid in a flask over a cross drawn on paper and times how long it takes for the cross to disappear: 20 °C: 160 s, 30 °C: 80 s, 40 °C: 40 s, 50 °C: 19 s, 60 °C: 10 s. The relative rate is found as 1000 ÷ time taken. Calculate the relative rate at 30 °C.

Felix mixes sodium thiosulfate solution with dilute hydrochloric acid in a flask over a cross drawn on paper and times how long it takes for the cross to disappear: 20 °C: 190 s, 30 °C: 100 s, 40 °C: 50 s, 50 °C: 26 s, 60 °C: 12 s. (a) Describe the relationship between temperature and the time taken. (b) Explain why the cross disappears. (c) Explain the effect of temperature using the particle model.
items.answer: (a) As temperature increases, the time decreases (roughly halving for every 10 °C rise), so the rate increases. (b) A yellow precipitate of sulfur forms and makes the mixture cloudy. (c) Particles move faster, so they collide more often and more collisions have enough energy to react.
items.markingKey: (a) higher temperature, shorter time [1] (b) precipitate / sulfur [1] (c) faster particles, more frequent and energetic collisions [1] [3]

items.stem: A food scientist in Dhaka finds that milk goes sour in about 2 days at 20 °C but in about 8 days at 5 °C. In a separate test, magnesium reacts with acid in 120 s at 25 °C and in 30 s at 45 °C. (a) Calculate how many times faster the magnesium reaction is at 45 °C than at 25 °C. (b) State two other variables that must be kept the same.
items.answer: (a) 4 times (b) Length (mass) of magnesium, volume and concentration of acid.
items.markingKey: (a) 120 ÷ 30 [1] = 4 [1] [2] (b) two variables [1] each [2]

items.stem: Why do particles collide more often at a higher temperature?
items.answer: They move faster
items.markingKey: More kinetic energy → faster movement → more frequent collisions.

items.stem: Explain why a reaction mixture is placed in a water bath during a rate investigation.
items.answer: To keep the temperature constant, because temperature affects the rate.
items.markingKey: constant temperature [1]; temperature affects rate [1] [2]

items.stem: Sofia mixes sodium thiosulfate solution with dilute hydrochloric acid in a flask over a cross drawn on paper and times how long it takes for the cross to disappear: 20 °C: 190 s, 30 °C: 100 s, 40 °C: 48 s, 50 °C: 25 s, 60 °C: 12 s. At which temperature is the reaction fastest?
items.markingKey: Shortest time = fastest rate.

items.stem: Grace mixes sodium thiosulfate solution with dilute hydrochloric acid in a flask over a cross drawn on paper and times how long it takes for the cross to disappear: 20 °C: 168 s, 30 °C: 80 s, 40 °C: 42 s, 50 °C: 20 s, 60 °C: 10 s. The relative rate is found as 1000 ÷ time taken. Calculate the relative rate at 20 °C.

A food scientist in Jakarta finds that milk goes sour in about 2 days at 20 °C but in about 8 days at 5 °C. In a separate test, magnesium reacts with acid in 120 s at 25 °C and in 30 s at 45 °C. (a) Calculate how many times faster the magnesium reaction is at 45 °C than at 25 °C. (b) Explain why food lasts longer in a refrigerator.
items.answer: (a) 4 times (b) Low temperature slows the reactions (of microorganisms and enzymes) that spoil food.
items.markingKey: (a) 120 ÷ 30 [1] = 4 [1] [2] (b) low temperature [1]; slower reactions [1] [2]

items.stem: A food scientist in Muscat finds that milk goes sour in about 2 days at 20 °C but in about 8 days at 5 °C. In a separate test, magnesium reacts with acid in 100 s at 25 °C and in 25 s at 45 °C. (a) Calculate how many times faster the magnesium reaction is at 45 °C than at 25 °C. (b) Explain the effect of temperature on rate using the particle model.
items.answer: (a) 4 times (b) At higher temperature particles have more kinetic energy, move faster, collide more often and more collisions have enough energy to react.
items.markingKey: (a) 100 ÷ 25 [1] = 4 [1] [2] (b) faster particles [1]; more frequent collisions [1]; more collisions with enough energy [1] [3]

items.stem: What happens to the rate of reaction when the concentration of an acid is increased?
items.answer: It increases
items.markingKey: More acid particles in the same volume → more frequent collisions.

items.stem: Explain, in terms of particles, why marble chips react faster in more concentrated acid.
items.answer: There are more acid particles in the same volume, so they collide with the marble surface more often.
items.markingKey: more particles per volume [1]; more frequent collisions [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why diluting acid with water slows its reaction with magnesium.
items.answer: The acid particles are more spread out, so collisions with magnesium are less frequent.
items.markingKey: particles more spread out [1]; fewer collisions [1] [2]

items.stem: Amara has hydrochloric acid of concentration 0.5 mol/dm³. To make weaker solutions, the acid is mixed with water so that the total volume is always 50 cm³. Calculate the volume of water needed with 40 cm³ of acid, and the new concentration.
items.answer: 10 cm³ of water; 0.4 mol/dm³

items.stem: Aisha has hydrochloric acid of concentration 1 mol/dm³. To make weaker solutions, the acid is mixed with water so that the total volume is always 50 cm³. A 2 cm strip of magnesium is added to each mixture and the time for fizzing to stop is recorded: 50 cm³ acid + 0 cm³ water: 29 s, 40 cm³ acid + 10 cm³ water: 35 s, 30 cm³ acid + 20 cm³ water: 48 s, 20 cm³ acid + 30 cm³ water: 72 s, 10 cm³ acid + 40 cm³ water: 144 s. (a) Calculate the concentration of the mixture with 10 cm³ of acid. (b) Describe the pattern in the results. (c) Explain the pattern using the particle model.
items.answer: (a) 0.2 mol/dm³ (b) The more concentrated the acid, the shorter the time (faster reaction). (c) More acid particles per cm³ collide with the magnesium more often.
items.markingKey: (a) 0.2 [1] (b) higher concentration, shorter time [1] (c) more frequent collisions [1] [3]

items.stem: Amara reacts marble chips with hydrochloric acid of two concentrations. With 1 mol/dm³ acid it takes 120 s to collect 60 cm³ of gas; with 2 mol/dm³ acid it takes 60 s. (a) Calculate the mean rate for each concentration. (b) Explain the result in terms of particles.
items.answer: (a) 0.5 cm³/s and 1 cm³/s (b) The more concentrated acid has twice as many acid particles per cm³, so collisions with the marble are twice as frequent.
items.markingKey: (a) 60 ÷ 120 = 0.5 [1]; 60 ÷ 60 = 1 [1] [2] (b) more particles per volume [1]; more frequent collisions [1] [2]

items.stem: A more concentrated solution has …
options: fewer particles in the same volume
faster particles at the same temperature
more particles in the same volume
items.answer: more particles in the same volume
items.markingKey: Concentration = amount of solute per unit volume.

items.stem: Explain why the total volume of water plus acid is kept the same when making different concentrations.
items.answer: So that only the concentration changes; a different total volume would change the amount of acid or the depth.
items.markingKey: only concentration varies [1]; fair test [1] [2]

items.stem: Nadia has hydrochloric acid of concentration 1 mol/dm³. To make weaker solutions, the acid is mixed with water so that the total volume is always 40 cm³. Calculate the volume of water needed with 10 cm³ of acid, and the new concentration.
items.answer: 30 cm³ of water; 0.25 mol/dm³

items.stem: Hana has hydrochloric acid of concentration 2 mol/dm³. To make weaker solutions, the acid is mixed with water so that the total volume is always 40 cm³. A 2 cm strip of magnesium is added to each mixture and the time for fizzing to stop is recorded: 40 cm³ acid + 0 cm³ water: 29 s, 30 cm³ acid + 10 cm³ water: 40 s, 20 cm³ acid + 20 cm³ water: 62 s, 10 cm³ acid + 30 cm³ water: 120 s. (a) Calculate the concentration of the mixture with 30 cm³ of acid. (b) Describe the pattern in the results. (c) Explain the pattern using the particle model.
items.answer: (a) 1.5 mol/dm³ (b) The more concentrated the acid, the shorter the time (faster reaction). (c) More acid particles per cm³ collide with the magnesium more often.
items.markingKey: (a) 1.5 [1] (b) higher concentration, shorter time [1] (c) more frequent collisions [1] [3]

items.stem: Grace has hydrochloric acid of concentration 1 mol/dm³. To make weaker solutions, the acid is mixed with water so that the total volume is always 40 cm³. A 2 cm strip of magnesium is added to each mixture and the time for fizzing to stop is recorded: 40 cm³ acid + 0 cm³ water: 31 s, 30 cm³ acid + 10 cm³ water: 43 s, 20 cm³ acid + 20 cm³ water: 64 s, 10 cm³ acid + 30 cm³ water: 124 s. (a) Calculate the concentration of the mixture with 30 cm³ of acid. (b) Describe the pattern in the results. (c) Explain the pattern using the particle model. (d) Explain why the total volume is kept constant.
items.answer: (a) 0.75 mol/dm³ (b) The more concentrated the acid, the shorter the time (faster reaction). (c) More acid particles per cm³ collide with the magnesium more often. (d) So only the concentration changes; it is a fair test.
items.markingKey: (a) 0.75 [1] (b) higher concentration, shorter time [1] (c) more frequent collisions [1] (d) fair test [1] [4]

items.stem: Noah reacts marble chips with hydrochloric acid of two concentrations. With 1 mol/dm³ acid it takes 96 s to collect 30 cm³ of gas; with 2 mol/dm³ acid it takes 48 s. (a) Calculate the mean rate for each concentration. (b) Describe the relationship between concentration and rate shown. (c) State two variables that must be controlled.
items.answer: (a) 0.313 cm³/s and 0.625 cm³/s (b) Doubling the concentration doubles the rate (rate is proportional to concentration here). (c) Mass and size of marble chips, volume of acid, temperature (any two).
items.markingKey: (a) 30 ÷ 96 = 0.313 [1]; 30 ÷ 48 = 0.625 [1] [2] (b) Doubling the concentration doubles the rate (rate is proportional to concentration here) [1] (c) two variables [1] each [2]

items.stem: What is the rate of a reaction?
options: How much product is formed in total
How quickly reactants are used up or products are formed
items.answer: How quickly reactants are used up or products are formed
items.markingKey: Rate = amount of product formed (or reactant used) ÷ time.

items.stem: Explain why the graph of gas volume against time becomes horizontal.
items.answer: The reaction has stopped because one reactant has been used up, so no more gas is produced.
items.markingKey: reaction stopped [1]; reactant used up [1] [2]

items.stem: In a test, Diego writes: "The balance reading falls because the marble disappears and mass is destroyed." Identify the error and give the correct science.
items.answer: Mass is conserved; it falls because carbon dioxide gas escapes from the flask.
items.markingKey: mass conserved [1]; gas escapes [1] [2]

items.stem: Mohammed places a flask of dilute hydrochloric acid and marble chips on a balance: 0 min: 168.75 g, 1 min: 167.76 g, 2 min: 167.10 g, 3 min: 166.65 g, 4 min: 166.36 g, 5 min: 166.16 g, 6 min: 166.02 g. Calculate the mass lost in the first 2 minutes and the mean rate of mass loss in g/min.

A class in Dubai reacts marble chips (calcium carbonate) with dilute hydrochloric acid and measures the carbon dioxide given off: 0 s: 0 cm³, 10 s: 24 cm³, 20 s: 38 cm³, 30 s: 47 cm³, 40 s: 52 cm³, 50 s: 55 cm³, 60 s: 57 cm³. (a) Calculate the mean rate of reaction in the first 10 s. (b) State the total volume of gas produced and estimate when the reaction finished.
items.answer: (a) 2.4 cm³/s (b) 57 cm³; at about 60 s

items.stem: Why does powder react faster than lumps of the same mass?
options: More particles are exposed for collisions
items.answer: More particles are exposed for collisions
items.markingKey: A larger surface area gives more frequent collisions.

items.stem: Explain why a fair test comparing chips and powder must use the same mass of solid.
items.answer: Changing the mass would change the amount of reactant, which also affects the rate and the volume of gas; only surface area should change.
items.markingKey: mass affects result [1]; only one variable changed [1] [2]

items.stem: A cube of calcium carbonate has sides of 3 cm. Calculate its total surface area.
items.answer: 54 cm²

items.stem: Jonas reacts 5 g of calcium carbonate with excess acid and times how long it takes to collect 100 cm³ of carbon dioxide: large lumps 200 s, small chips 120 s, powder 30 s. Calculate the mean rate of reaction for the lumps and for the powder.
items.answer: 0.5 cm³/s and 3.33 cm³/s

items.stem: In a flour mill in Madrid, a safety officer warns that fine flour dust in the air could explode. (a) Suggest one advantage and one disadvantage of a fast-acting powder. (b) Explain whether the total volume of gas produced depends on the form used.
items.answer: (a) Advantage: relieves symptoms quickly. Disadvantage: harder to measure a dose, may fizz over, absorbs moisture from air. (b) No: the same mass contains the same amount of reactant, so the total is the same; only the rate changes.
items.markingKey: (a) advantage [1]; disadvantage [1] [2] (b) same total [1]; same amount of reactant [1] [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Food is kept in a fridge because … (b) For a reaction to happen, particles must …
items.answer: (a) reactions that spoil food are slower at low temperature (b) collide with enough energy
items.markingKey: (a) Lower temperature slows the reactions of decay microorganisms. (b) Only collisions with enough energy are successful.

items.stem: Explain why the disappearing cross experiment uses the same depth of solution each time.
items.answer: The time for the cross to disappear depends on how much liquid it is viewed through; same depth keeps it a fair test.
items.markingKey: depth affects visibility [1]; fair test [1] [2]

items.stem: Diego mixes sodium thiosulfate solution with dilute hydrochloric acid in a flask over a cross drawn on paper and times how long it takes for the cross to disappear: 20 °C: 133 s, 30 °C: 70 s, 40 °C: 33 s, 50 °C: 18 s, 60 °C: 9 s. The relative rate is found as 1000 ÷ time taken. Calculate the relative rate at 20 °C.

Aisha mixes sodium thiosulfate solution with dilute hydrochloric acid in a flask over a cross drawn on paper and times how long it takes for the cross to disappear: 20 °C: 190 s, 30 °C: 100 s, 40 °C: 52 s, 50 °C: 24 s, 60 °C: 12 s. (a) Describe the relationship between temperature and the time taken. (b) Explain why the cross disappears. (c) Explain the effect of temperature using the particle model.
items.answer: (a) As temperature increases, the time decreases (roughly halving for every 10 °C rise), so the rate increases. (b) A yellow precipitate of sulfur forms and makes the mixture cloudy. (c) Particles move faster, so they collide more often and more collisions have enough energy to react.
items.markingKey: (a) higher temperature, shorter time [1] (b) precipitate / sulfur [1] (c) faster particles, more frequent and energetic collisions [1] [3]

items.answer: (a) 4 times (b) At higher temperature particles have more kinetic energy, move faster, collide more often and more collisions have enough energy to react.
items.markingKey: (a) 120 ÷ 30 [1] = 4 [1] [2] (b) faster particles [1]; more frequent collisions [1]; more collisions with enough energy [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain why a reaction between marble and acid slows down even though the marble is in excess.
items.answer: The acid is used up, so its concentration falls and collisions become less frequent.
items.markingKey: acid concentration falls [1]; fewer collisions [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why concentrated acids are more hazardous than dilute ones.
items.answer: They react faster and more vigorously with skin and materials, causing more damage more quickly.
items.markingKey: faster reaction [1]; more damage [1] [2]

items.stem: Mohammed has hydrochloric acid of concentration 1 mol/dm³. To make weaker solutions, the acid is mixed with water so that the total volume is always 40 cm³. Calculate the volume of water needed with 30 cm³ of acid, and the new concentration.
items.answer: 10 cm³ of water; 0.75 mol/dm³

items.stem: Chloe has hydrochloric acid of concentration 1 mol/dm³. To make weaker solutions, the acid is mixed with water so that the total volume is always 50 cm³. A 2 cm strip of magnesium is added to each mixture and the time for fizzing to stop is recorded: 50 cm³ acid + 0 cm³ water: 29 s, 40 cm³ acid + 10 cm³ water: 36 s, 30 cm³ acid + 20 cm³ water: 45 s, 20 cm³ acid + 30 cm³ water: 70 s, 10 cm³ acid + 40 cm³ water: 144 s. (a) Calculate the concentration of the mixture with 40 cm³ of acid. (b) Describe the pattern in the results. (c) Explain the pattern using the particle model.
items.answer: (a) 0.8 mol/dm³ (b) The more concentrated the acid, the shorter the time (faster reaction). (c) More acid particles per cm³ collide with the magnesium more often.
items.markingKey: (a) 0.8 [1] (b) higher concentration, shorter time [1] (c) more frequent collisions [1] [3]

items.stem: A technician in Nairobi compares two bottles of acid, 1 mol/dm³ and 2 mol/dm³. Using the same marble chips, 40 cm³ of carbon dioxide is collected in 80 s and 40 s respectively. (a) Explain the result in terms of particles. (b) State two variables that must be controlled. (c) Sketch or describe the graph of volume against time for both concentrations if the marble is in excess.
items.answer: (a) The more concentrated acid has twice as many acid particles per cm³, so collisions with the marble are twice as frequent. (b) Mass and size of marble chips, volume of acid, temperature (any two). (c) Both curves start at zero; the higher concentration curve is steeper and levels off sooner; the higher concentration gives twice the final volume because more acid is present.
items.markingKey: (a) more particles per volume [1]; more frequent collisions [1] [2] (b) two variables [1] each [2] (c) steeper for higher conc [1]; final volumes reflect acid amount [1] [2]

items.stem: Which unit could be used for the rate of a reaction that produces a gas?
items.answer: cm³/s
items.markingKey: Volume of gas per unit time.

items.stem: Explain how you can use a graph to compare the rates of two reactions.
items.answer: The steeper curve shows the faster reaction; the one that reaches its final volume sooner is faster.
items.markingKey: steeper = faster [1]; finishes sooner [1] [2]

items.stem: In a test, Ana writes: "The reaction is fastest at the end because the most gas has been collected by then." Identify the error and give the correct science.
items.answer: The total volume is largest at the end, but the rate (gas per second) is greatest at the start, where the graph is steepest.
items.markingKey: total vs rate [1]; steepest at start [1] [2]

items.stem: Daniel adds magnesium ribbon to dilute hydrochloric acid and collects the hydrogen in a gas syringe: 0 s: 0 cm³, 15 s: 47 cm³, 30 s: 70 cm³, 45 s: 81 cm³, 60 s: 86 cm³, 75 s: 88 cm³, 90 s: 89 cm³. Calculate the mean rate of reaction over the first 30 s.
items.answer: 2.33 cm³/s

items.stem: A class in Accra reacts magnesium ribbon with dilute hydrochloric acid and measures the hydrogen given off: 0 s: 0 cm³, 20 s: 38 cm³, 40 s: 52 cm³, 60 s: 57 cm³, 80 s: 59 cm³, 100 s: 60 cm³, 120 s: 60 cm³. (a) Calculate the mean rate of reaction in the first 20 s. (b) State the total volume of gas produced and estimate when the reaction finished.
items.answer: (a) 1.9 cm³/s (b) 60 cm³; at about 80 s

items.stem: Breaking a cube into eight smaller cubes makes the total surface area …
items.answer: twice as large
items.markingKey: Each small cube has 1/4 the face area; 8 × 1/4 = 2 times.

items.stem: Omar says: "Powder gives off more gas in total than chips." Explain why Omar is wrong.
items.answer: With the same mass and excess acid, both give the same total volume; powder just produces it faster.
items.markingKey: same total [1]; faster [1] [2]

items.stem: Samuel reacts 5 g of calcium carbonate with excess acid and times how long it takes to collect 80 cm³ of carbon dioxide: large lumps 240 s, small chips 120 s, powder 30 s. Calculate the mean rate of reaction for the lumps and for the powder.
items.answer: 0.333 cm³/s and 2.67 cm³/s

items.stem: Mateo reacts 5 g of calcium carbonate with excess acid and times how long it takes to collect 100 cm³ of carbon dioxide: large lumps 300 s, small chips 120 s, powder 30 s. Calculate the mean rate of reaction for the lumps and for the powder.
items.answer: 0.333 cm³/s and 3.33 cm³/s

items.stem: In a flour mill in Colombo, a safety officer warns that fine flour dust in the air could explode. (a) Explain why the powder form reacts fastest. (b) Explain whether the total volume of gas produced depends on the form used.
items.answer: (a) It has the largest surface area, so more particles are exposed for collisions. (b) No: the same mass contains the same amount of reactant, so the total is the same; only the rate changes.
items.markingKey: (a) surface area [1]; more frequent collisions [1] [2] (b) same total [1]; same amount of reactant [1] [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Why do particles collide more often at a higher temperature? (b) As a rough rule, a 10 °C rise in temperature makes many reactions go about …
items.answer: (a) They move faster (b) twice as fast
items.markingKey: (a) More kinetic energy → faster movement → more frequent collisions. (b) Rate approximately doubles per 10 °C rise.

items.stem: Explain why a reaction that is safe at 20 °C may become dangerous if heated strongly.
items.answer: The rate increases a lot, so gas or heat may be produced too fast to control.
items.markingKey: rate increases greatly [1]; gas/heat released too fast [1] [2]

items.stem: Yusuf mixes sodium thiosulfate solution with dilute hydrochloric acid in a flask over a cross drawn on paper and times how long it takes for the cross to disappear: 20 °C: 189 s, 30 °C: 94 s, 40 °C: 47 s, 50 °C: 22 s, 60 °C: 12 s. The relative rate is found as 1000 ÷ time taken. Calculate the relative rate at 50 °C.

Zara mixes sodium thiosulfate solution with dilute hydrochloric acid in a flask over a cross drawn on paper and times how long it takes for the cross to disappear: 20 °C: 189 s, 30 °C: 86 s, 40 °C: 45 s, 50 °C: 21 s, 60 °C: 11 s. (a) Describe the relationship between temperature and the time taken. (b) Explain why the cross disappears. (c) Explain the effect of temperature using the particle model.
items.answer: (a) As temperature increases, the time decreases (roughly halving for every 10 °C rise), so the rate increases. (b) A yellow precipitate of sulfur forms and makes the mixture cloudy. (c) Particles move faster, so they collide more often and more collisions have enough energy to react.
items.markingKey: (a) higher temperature, shorter time [1] (b) precipitate / sulfur [1] (c) faster particles, more frequent and energetic collisions [1] [3]

items.stem: Diego reacts a 3 cm length of magnesium ribbon with dilute hydrochloric acid. At 25 °C the fizzing stops after 100 s; at 45 °C it stops after 25 s. (a) Explain the effect of temperature on rate using the particle model. (b) State two other variables that must be kept the same.
items.answer: (a) At higher temperature particles have more kinetic energy, move faster, collide more often and more collisions have enough energy to react. (b) Length (mass) of magnesium, volume and concentration of acid.
items.markingKey: (a) faster particles [1]; more frequent collisions [1]; more collisions with enough energy [1] [3] (b) two variables [1] each [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why concentrated acids are more hazardous than dilute ones. (b) Explain why the total volume of water plus acid is kept the same when making different concentrations.
items.answer: (a) They react faster and more vigorously with skin and materials, causing more damage more quickly. (b) So that only the concentration changes; a different total volume would change the amount of acid or the depth.
items.markingKey: (a) faster reaction [1]; more damage [1] [2] (b) only concentration varies [1]; fair test [1] [2]

items.stem: Leila claims: "Doubling the concentration doubles the total volume of gas, even if the acid is in excess." Do you agree? Explain your answer.
items.answer: No. If the acid is in excess, the total gas depends on the other reactant; concentration changes only the rate.
items.markingKey: total set by limiting reactant [1]; rate changes [1] [2]

items.stem: Omar has hydrochloric acid of concentration 0.5 mol/dm³. To make weaker solutions, the acid is mixed with water so that the total volume is always 50 cm³. Calculate the volume of water needed with 30 cm³ of acid, and the new concentration.
items.answer: 20 cm³ of water; 0.3 mol/dm³

items.stem: Noah has hydrochloric acid of concentration 1 mol/dm³. To make weaker solutions, the acid is mixed with water so that the total volume is always 100 cm³. A 2 cm strip of magnesium is added to each mixture and the time for fizzing to stop is recorded: 100 cm³ acid + 0 cm³ water: 33 s, 80 cm³ acid + 20 cm³ water: 41 s, 60 cm³ acid + 40 cm³ water: 53 s, 40 cm³ acid + 60 cm³ water: 82 s, 20 cm³ acid + 80 cm³ water: 160 s. (a) Calculate the concentration of the mixture with 60 cm³ of acid. (b) Describe the pattern in the results. (c) Explain the pattern using the particle model.
items.answer: (a) 0.6 mol/dm³ (b) The more concentrated the acid, the shorter the time (faster reaction). (c) More acid particles per cm³ collide with the magnesium more often.
items.markingKey: (a) 0.6 [1] (b) higher concentration, shorter time [1] (c) more frequent collisions [1] [3]
